## ABSTRACT

Bacteria in biological wastewater treatment process play an important role in the removal of substrate concentration. When bacteria removes the substrate, they continuously growth until such time when the substrate concentration is depleted. This paper aims to review the performance of kinetic growth rate models that describe specific bacteria growth rate. The kinetic growth rate models reviewed were: Monod, Blackman, Haldane, Teissier, Moser, Contois, Logarithmic, Powell, Han and Levenspiel, Logistic, Luong, Webb, Yano and Koga, and Aiba-Edwards. The performance review of the models were based on coefficient of determination ( $ R^{2} $). Another statistical measure of performance was root mean square error (RMSE). All kinetic growth rate models performed well when subjected to both toxic and non-toxic substrate concentration. The most notable kinetic growth rate model was the Haldane model which was well represented in the literature.

## Introduction

In biological wastewater treatment process, bacteria are used to oxidise dissolved and particulate carbonaceous organic matter into simple end products. The organic matter present is composed of domestic and industrial waste and is usually referred to as substrate (Choi et al. (2017), and Metcalf and Eddy, (2003)). In addition to substrate, oxygen is required to complete biological wastewater treatment process. The biological wastewater treatment process can be expressed by reaction equation 1.

Bacterial growth can be described in 4 phases: Lag phase, Exponential phase, Stationary phase, and death phase. In the lag phase, bacteria take time to acclimatize to their new environment in the bioreactor. While the acclimatizing process takes place, there is no growth of bacteria in the bioreactor. The exponential growth phase is the most rapid growth possible. During this phase, the bacteria present in the bioreactor doubles at a high rate. The stationary phase defines the no growth phase. Although there is no growth in the stationary phase, the bacteria continue to multiple while some continue to die. The stationary phase occurs due to the depletion of essential nutrients, and presence of toxic substrate. The last phase is the death phase. In the death phase, nutrients required for bacterial growth are completely used up. The 4 phases are described in Fig. 1. ((Metcalf and Eddy, (2003), Maier and Pepper (2015)).

Bacteria growth is determined using Eq. (2). Eq. (2) requires the measurement of biomass concentration at different time intervals. There are two common methods used to determine biomass concentration: Cell dry weight mass method and the Optical density (OD) method. The cell dry weight mass method has the advantage of providing direct unconditional estimates. The disadvantage of the cell dry weight mass method is interference from dead cells and non-cell solids. Further-more the method is time consuming and labour intense (Panikov, 2009). The OD method has the advantage of its simplicity, quickness, and automation. The disadvantage of the OD method is the interference with non-cell solids. The OD method measures the absorbance of the sample using a spectrophotometer at a wavelength between 540 - 600 nm. A calibration curve of absorbance and cell dry weight mass is required to relate absorbance with cell dry weight mass. In other words, cell dry weight mass method for each culture is required at least once when using the OD method. OD measurements are then converted to biomass concentration using the calibrated curve (Panikov (2009), and Wang (2009)).

concentration. There are different types of kinetic growth models used to describe specific bacteria growth rate in biological wastewater treatment process. These methods can be further divided into structured and unstructured kinetic growth models. Structured kinetic growth models incorporate genetic, morphological, or biochemical attributes that collectively determine the physiological state of the biomass. Although structured kinetic growth models are capable of describing specific growth rate of the bacteria, they are complicated and they require a number of equations to solve (Dong et al., 2015; Mrwebi (2004); Panikov (2009)). Unstructured growth models view bacteria as independent organisms which interact with the environment. Unstructured kinetic growth models describe bacteria growth rate based on biomass and substrate concentration (Dong et al., 2015; Mrwebi (2004); Panikov (2009)). Unstructured kinetic growth models are more suitable for steady state balance while structured models are more suitable for unsteady state balance (Panikov, 2009).

One of the earliest kinetic growth models used to describe specific growth rate is the Monod model (Monod, 1942). Later on, it was found that the Monod model was not capable of describing specific growth rate in the presence of toxic substrate concentration. ((Haldane, 1965), (Luong, 1987), and (Aiba et al., 1968)). At high substrate concentration, nutrients inhibit the growth of bacteria due to toxic substrate.

The kinetic growth models were evaluated using coefficient of determination ( $ R^{2} $).  $ R^{2} $ is defined as the ratio of the explained variation to the total variation. Gharibzahedi et al., (2013) explained that  $ R^{2} $ is used to determine the efficiency of the model and its closeness to a value of 1 is an effective and practical measure of the validity of a model prediction. On the contrary, Ford, (2015) Statistical Research Consultant at the University of Virginia reported that  $ R^{2} $ cannot be used as a measure of goodness to fit, predictive error, and cannot be used to compare models. One of the error functions used to check the robustness of a model is by determining root mean square error (RMSE). RMSE is the standard deviation of the residual. Residuals are a measure of how far from the regression line data points are (Sharifahmadian, 2015) Chai and Draxler (2014). This paper aims to review the performance of 14 unstructured kinetic growth models that are used to describe specific bacteria growth rate. The models reviewed are: Monod, Blackman, Haldane, Teissier, Moser, Contois, Logarithmic, Powell, Han and Levenspiel, Logistic, Luong, Webb, Yano and Koga, and Aiba-Edwards. This paper is organised as follows: section 2 introduces unstructured kinetic growth models, section 3 discusses the unstructured kinetic growth models, and section 4 details the conclusion.

## Unstructured models

Kinetic growth models are useful because they assist engineers to design and control biological processes (Dong et al., 2015). In the literature reviewed, there are 2 types of unstructured kinetic growth models, those that account for substrate inhibition and non-substrate inhibition (Annuar et al., 2008). Table 1 shows a list of the kinetic growth models and description. The parameter constants of all the kinetic growth models are estimated using nonlinear least of squares.

## Discussions

## Monod model

The Monod model was first introduced by Jacques Monod in 1942 to describe the relationship between specific growth rate and substrate utilization rate in a bioreactor (Monod, 1949). The model can be defined in two forms: based on substrate concentration only, and based on both substrate and biomass concentration. The two forms of the model are defined by Eqs. (3) and 4.

Where,  $ \mu_{max} $ maximum bacteria growth rate, S substrate concentration,  $ K_{s} $ half saturation constant,  $ \mu $ specific bacteria growth rate, and X biomass concentration. The maximum bacteria growth rate and half saturation constant are constants. The Monod model assumes that there is only one growth limiting substrate in the bioreactor (Monod, 1942). The Monod model has 5 limitations as described by Kong (2017). The 1st limitation is observed at high substrate concentration. At high substrate concentration, the maximum specific growth rate is independent of the substrate concentration. The 2nd limitation is observed at low substrate concentration. At low substrate concentration, growth is dependent on substrate concentration. 3rd limitation is that the Monod model cannot be applied when a substrate exhibits inhibition (Kim et al., (2005); Shukor (2014); Han and Levenspiel (1988)). Toxic substrate that can be found in industrial wastewater can hinder bacteria growth and substrate consumption (Shukor, 2014), and (Mahanta et al., 2014). The 4th limitation is that the Monod model does not account for the fact that cells may require substrate for maintenance during the death phase. The 5th limitation is that the model does not account for the lag and death phase during the growth phase (Kong (2017), and Mrwebi (2004)).

The limitations described above were evident on literature reported below. Hamitouche et al., (2012) reported a poor fit on biodegradation of phenol by mixed culture in a batch reactor. The growth rates were measured using Optical density (OD) at 600 nm to describe the specific growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 52%. Debasmita and Rajasimman (2013) reported a poor fit on biodegradation of atrazine using mixed microorganisms. The growth rates were measured using OD at 600 nm to describe the specific growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 30.4%. Ahmad et al., (2015) reported a poor fit on biodegradation kinetics of Caffeine by Leifsonia sp. strain SIU. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 47.9%. Abubakar et al., (2017) reported a poor fit on growth kinetics of Tributytin-Resistant Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 in Cadmium Media. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 53.4%. Abdullah et al., (2006) reported a poor fit on cell growth kinetics of Aspergillus oryzae in industrial natural rubber effluent serum. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 65.3%. Abdussamad et al., (2017) reported a poor fit on growth kinetics of Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 on TBT-Resistant containing Lead. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 75.4%. Ardestani and Kasebkar (2018) reported a poor fit on Aspergillus niger growth and substrate uptake in a batch submerged culture. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 77.7%. It was expected of the Monod model to struggle with describing kinetic growth rate on the literature above because the substrate utilised have been described to exhibit inhibition of cell growth (Ku et al., 2011; Hashimoto et al., 2004).

Despite the poor fit of the Monod model on the literature mentioned above, the model still remains the most widely used to describe specific growth rate and substrate utilization rate (Rajasekar et al., (2015), Ravi et al., (2013); Dong et al., (2015); Rodríguez-Gómez et al., (2014)). The literature reported below showed satisfactory fit of the Monod model. Ardestani (2011) reported a satisfactory fit of the Monod model on the study of Penicillium brevicompectum ATCC 16,024 cell growth. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 87%. Ardestani and Shafiei (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on the cell growth of Saccharomyces cerevisiae in a batch culture. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 81%. Wu et al., (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on cyanide degradation in a microbial fuel cell. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 84.2%. Mahanta et al., (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on the study of Escherichia coli. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 99.6%. Krishnan et al., (2017) reported a satisfactory fit on biodegradation kinetics of Azo dye Mixture. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 99.9%. Annuar et al., (2008) reported a satisfactory fit on growth and biosynthesis of medium-chain-length poly-(3-hydroxyalkanoates) in Pseudomonas putida. The 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 90.9%. Ahmad et al., (2011) reported a satisfactory fit on Ethanol production by Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 95.7%. Costa et al., (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on the degradation of Diethyl-ketone by Streptococcus equisimilis. The OD at 620 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 80%. Dey and Mukherjee (2010) reported a satisfactory fit on Phenol biodegradation by mixed microbial culture in a batch reactor. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced root mean square of 0.0208. Gharibzahedi et al., (2013) reported a satisfactory fit on cell growth and canthaxanthin biosynthesis by Dietzia natronolimnaea. The OD at

600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ 93%. The Monod model performed well when tested on phenol, azo dye, ethanol, and cyanide which have been reported to exhibit cell inhibition (Wu et al., (2018); Krishnan et al., (2017); Ahmad et al., (2011)).

## Blackman model

The Blackman model was introduced by Blackman in 1905 (Blackman, 1905). The model is similar to the Monod model in terms of its assumptions. At low substrate concentration, growth is dependent on substrate and at high substrate concentration, growth is independent of substrate concentration. At high substrate concentration, some nutrients are limiting (Kong, 2017). The model has been described as being capable of making a sharp transition from first order kinetics to zero order kinetics (Mrwebi, 2004). Blackman model is defined by equation 5.

Where,  $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate, S substrate concentration, and  $ K_{s} $ half saturation constant. Just like the Monod model, the Blackman model is unable to capture the lag and death phase, and in turn it over estimates the specific growth rate (Kong, 2017). The Blackman model is not a popular method for modelling growth rate in microbial processes, and when utilized it performed poorly. Mahanta et al., (2014) reported results on the comparison between Blackman, Monod, Powell, and Moser models. In the study the Blackman model was the only model that did not fit the experimental data with a reported  $ R^{2} $ of 43.3%. The Blackman model has been shadowed by models such as the Monod model.

## Haldane model

The Haldane model was introduced by Haldane in 1930. The model is viewed as an extension of the Monod model. The model introduces a 3rd constant  $ K_{i} $ that deals with specific growth rate inhibition at low and high substrate concentration.  $ K_{i} $ is the inhibition constant which is equal to the highest substrate concentration at which the specific growth rate is equal to one half maximum growth rate in the absence of an inhibition. Kong (2017) reported that at high substrate concentration, specific growth rate of an organism may be hindered by the presence of toxic substrate. With the inclusion of the inhibition constant, the model is capable of handling both toxic and non-toxic substrate. The Haldane model is defined by equation 6.

Where,  $ \mu $ specific growth rate,  $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate,  $ K_s $ half saturation constant,  $ S $ substrate concentration, and  $ K_i $ inhibition constant. The advantage of the Haldane model is that it is capable of describing all growth phases: lag, exponential, stationary, and death phase (Dutta et al., 2015). Due to its ability to describe growth rate at low and high substrate concentration, the Haldane model was the popular model used by many researchers (Shukor (2014); Dutta et al., (2015) Dey and Mukherjee, 2010).

The Haldane model has been hardly found waiting when being fitted to any experimental data. Wu et al., (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on kinetics and electro genesis change during cyanide degradation in a microbial fuel cell. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 98.6%. Saravanan et al., (2008) reported satisfactory fit on the growth kinetics of an indigenous mixed microbial consortium during phenol degradation. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced RMSE of 0.2020. Ibrahim et al., (2016) reported a satisfactory fit on growth kinetic studies of caffeine-degrading bacterium. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 90%. The results reported by Ibrahim et al., (2016) differed from the one reported by Ahmad et al., (2015). Ahmad et al., (2015) reported a poor fit on biodegradation of Caffeine. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 74.4%. Mohanty et al., (2018) reported satisfactory fit on effects of phenol on sulphate reduction by mixed microbial culture. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 81%. Halmi et al., (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on catechol-degrading candida parapsilosis. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 99.6%.

Hamitouche et al., (2012) reported satisfactory fit on the biodegradation of phenol by mixed culture. The growth rates were measured using Optical density (OD) at 600 nm to describe the specific growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 87%. Dey and Mukherjee (2010) reported a satisfactory fit on the performance and kinetic evaluation of phenol biodegradation by mixed microbial culture. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced RMSE of 0.0067. Debasmita and Rajasimman (2013) reported satisfactory fit on biodegradation of atrazine using mixed microorganisms. The growth rates were measured using OD at 600 nm to describe the specific growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 90%. Costa et al., (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on the degradation of diethyl-ketone by Streptococcus equisimilis. The OD at 620 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 98%. Choi and Lee (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on micro-algal biomass/bioenergy production with agricultural by-products. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 89.9%. Carrera et al., (2004) reported satisfactory fit on kinetic models for nitrification inhibition by ammonium and nitrite in a suspended and an immobilised biomass systems. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 93.7%. Gharibzahedi et al., (2013) reported a satisfactory fit on cell growth and canthaxanthin biosynthesis by Dietzia natronolimnaea. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 93.1%. Abubakar et al., (2017) reported a satisfactory fit on growth kinetics of Tributyitin-Resistant Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 in cadmium Media. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 92.6%.

Abdussamad et al., (2017) reported a satisfactory fit on growth kinetics of Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 on TBT-Resistant containing Lead. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 96%. Shukor (2014) and Kong (2017) reported a satisfactory fit on Bacillus sp containing chromate. The Haldane model produced RMSE and  $ R^{2} $ of 0.0004 and 95.6% respectively. Raghuvanshi and Babu reported a satisfactory fit on the removal of methyl ethyl-ketone substrate. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 87%. Ravi et al., (2013) reported satisfactory fit on the degradation of the methylene chloride. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 94.7%. Krishnan et al., (2017) reported experimental data fit on biodegradation kinetics of Azo dye Mixture. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 90.5%. On the other hand, Dutta et al., (2015) reported a poor fit on growth kinetics for Cutinase producing Pseudomonas Cepacia using tomato-peel extracted cutin. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Haldane model produced  $ R^{2} $ 57%. The Haldane model has performed well based on the literature reported above. The only challenge was experienced on the biodegradation of phenol, where it average an  $ R^{2} $ of 85%. Overall the performance of the Haldane model was good enough.

## Teissier model

The Teissier model was introduced in 1942 (Teissier, 1942). The author is sometimes referred to as Tessier. The Teissier model is also known as the Exponential model that describes the specific growth rate as a function of continuous substrate concentration. The model is similar to the Monod model, and Blackman model. Experimental data fitted on the Teissier model was observed to lie in between the Monod model, and Blackman model (Kong, 2017). Just like the Monod model, Blackman model, and Moser model, the Teissier model is not capable of describing cell growth inhibition. Hence it is not capable of describing the lag and death phase. The Teissier model is defined by equation 7.

Where,  $ \mu $ specific growth rate,  $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate,  $ K_T $ proportional constant, S substrate concentration. The Teissier model differs with the Monod model, Blackman model, and Moser model when it transitions from first order kinetics to zero order kinetics (Kong (2017); Dey and Mukherjee (2010), and Dutta et al., (2015)). Literature has shown that the Teissier model is capable of describing specific growth rate in different substrate concentrations.

Krishnan et al., (2017) reported a satisfactory fit on biodegradation kinetics of Azo dye Mixture. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 98.2%. Dey and Mukherjee (2010) reported a satisfactory fit on phenol biodegradation by mixed microbial culture in a batch reactor. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced RMSE of 0.0075. Sadhukhan et al., (2016) reported a satisfactory fit on microbial production of succinic acid using crude and purified glycerol. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced RMSE of 0.225. Choi and Lee (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on micro-algal biomass/bioenergy production with agricultural by-products. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 92.5%. Ahmad et al., (2011) reported a satisfactory fit on growth kinetic and modelling of ethanol production by Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 96.3%. Annuar et al., (2008) reported a satisfactory fit on the growth of Pseudomonas putida with ammonium as a growth limiting substrate. The 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 95.6%. Sun et al., (2009) reported a satisfactory fit on the degradation of pharmaceuticals in wastewater treatment. The 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 99.5%. Abdullah et al., (2006) reported a satisfactory fit on Aspergillus oryzae in industrial natural rubber effluent serum. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 83.6%. The Teissier model performed well when subjected to substrate that exhibits cell growth such as Azo dye, phenol, ethanol, ammonium, and succinic acid.

On the other hand, Abdussamad et al., (2017) reported a poor fit on growth kinetics of Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 on TBT-resistant containing Lead. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 42%. Abubakar et al., (2017) reported a poor fit on growth kinetics of Tributytin-Resistant Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 in cadmium Media. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 59.5%. Ahmad et al., (2015) reported a poor fit on biodegradation kinetics of caffeine. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 68%. Debasmita and Rajasimman (2013) reported a poor fit on biodegradation of Atrazine using mixed microorganisms. The growth rates were measured using OD at 600 nm to describe the specific growth rates. The Teissier model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 31.5%. Although the Teissier model was able to fit experimental data on phenol, ethanol, and ammonium, it struggled with fitting data on substrate that exhibits cell inhibition such as lead, cadmium, caffeine, and atrazine. The performance of the model is unpredictable and it may rely on the sampling methods, and data analysing methods.

## The moser model

The Moser model is an unstructured model based on substrate concentration only introduced in 1958 by Herman Moser (Moser, 1958). The model is an extension of the Monod model. The Moser model introduced a parameter constant (n) on the Monod model. The parameter (n) is an adjustable parameter that provides flexibility in fitting experimental data and dynamic behaviour in the bioreactor (Mahanta et al., 2014). The Moser model is considered to be a better model than the Monod model because the parameter (n) can be adjusted to fit the experimental data (Kong, 2017). The Moser model can be defined by equation 8.

Where  $ \mu $ specific growth rate,  $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate, S substrate concentration,  $ K_{s} $ half saturation constant, and n adjustable parameter. Just like the Blackman model, and Contois model, the Moser model has not been widely used to describe specific growth rate. The Moser model does not consider substrate inhibition, hence it cannot deal with toxic substrate. On the contrary, Krishnan et al., (2017) reported that the parameter (n) of the Moser model is used to describe substrate inhibition. Unlike the Monod model, and Contois model, the Moser model is capable of describing the lag phase when substrate concentration is high (Kong, 2017). The Moser model cannot describe the death phase.

Literature has shown good performance of the Moser model when fitted on different types of experimental data. Annuar et al., (2008) reported satisfactory fit on biosynthesis of medium-chain-length poly(3-hydroxyalkanoates) in Pseudomonas putida. The 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 95.7%. Choi and Lee (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on micro-algal biomass/bioenergy production with agricultural by-products. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 96%. Dutta et al., (2015) reported a satisfactory fit on Cutinase producing Pseudomonas cepacia using tomato-peel extracted cutin. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 85.5%. Gharibzahedi et al., (2013) reported a satisfactory fit on cell growth and Canthaxanthin biosynthesis by Dietzia natronolimnaea HS-1. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 94.9%. Halmi et al., (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on catechol-degradation. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 99.2%. Krishnan et al., (2017) reported satisfactory fit on biodegradation of Azo dye mixture. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 96.1%. Sadhukhan et al., (2016) reported a satisfactory fit on microbial production of succinic acid using crude and purified glycerol from a crotalaria juncea. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced RMSE 0.227. Mahanta et al., (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on E. coli. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 99.96%. Ardestani (2011) reported a satisfactory fit on cell growth Pseudomonas putida ATCC 16,024. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 87%. Ardestani and Shafiei (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on Saccharomyces cerevisiae cell growth. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 97%. Ardestani and Kasebkar (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on

Aspergillus niger PTCC 5010 in a batch culture. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 91.3%. On the other hand, Debasmita and Rajasimman (2013) reported a poor fit on biodegradation of Atrazine using mixed microorganisms. The growth rates were measured using OD at 600 nm to describe the specific growth rates. The Moser model produced  $ R^{2} $ 0.39%. The Moser model performed well on substrate that exhibits cell inhibition such as Azo dye, agricultural products, and succinic acid. The parameter n assisted when the model was subjected to toxic substrate.

The Contois model was introduced in 1959 (Contois, 1959). The model is an extension of the Monod model. The model is an unstructured model based on both substrate and biomass concentration (Ardestani and Kasebkar, 2018). The Contois model can be defined by equation 9.

The Contois model takes a different approach when compared to the Monod model, Blackman model, and the Moser model. In the Contois model, the assumption is that biomass concentration is inversely proportional to specific growth rate. Just like the Monod model, Blackman model, and Teissier model, the Contois model cannot describe the lag and death phase. Hence it does not capture substrate inhibition. The Contois model has not been widely used to describe specific growth rate, and when used, it produced satisfactory fit on the experimental data (Mrwebi, 2004). Abdullah et al., (2006) reported a satisfactory fit on Aspergillus oryzae in industrial natural rubber effluent serum. The Contois model produced  $ R^2 $ of 80.2%. The Contois model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98.4%. On the other hand, Ardestani (2011) reported a poor fit on cell growth Pseudomonas putida ATCC 16,024. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Contois model produced  $ R^2 $ of 75%. Ardestani and Kasebkar (2018) reported a poor fit on Aspergillus niger growth. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Contois model produced  $ R^2 $ of 75.1%. The Contois model performed well when it was fitted on experimental data of different substrate concentration. Although the Contois model has been described as not being capable of handling cell growth inhibition, literature reported above showed that it was capable. The Contois model handled ethanol, and industrial natural rubber as reported by Ahmad et al., (2015), and Abdullah et al., (2006). The two substrate types were reported to exhibit cell inhibition. The performance of the Contois model can be unpredicted as reported in the literature above.

## Logarithmic model

The logarithmic model was introduced by Westerhoff et al., (1982). The model describes specific growth rate as a function of logarithm of substrate concentration. The Logarithmic model is the worse model when compared with models discussed above because it is not capable of describing the lag, stationary, and death phase. The model has a reputation of over estimating cell growth, and if the substrate concentration is low, it can produce negative growth rate (Kong, 2017). This is a set back because growth cannot be classified as negative, and hence the Logarithmic model is not well represented in literature. The model is defined by equation 10.

The Logarithmic model is defined by Eq. (10). Where, a and b are constants, and s substrate concentration. The non-existence of literature reported for this model makes it difficult to make judgement on the performance of the model.

The inhibitory constant accounts for the presence of toxic substrate concentration in the bioreactor. With the ability to handle toxic substrate, the model is capable of describing the lag and death phase (Kong, 2017). The model is defined by equation 11.

The Aiba-Edward model produced  $ R^2 $ of 91%. Carrera et al., (2004) reported a satisfactory fit by ammonium and nitrite in a suspended and an immobilised biomass systems of the Aiba-Edward model. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Aiba-Edward model produced  $ R^2 $ of 82%. Annuar et al., (2008) reported a satisfactory fit of medium-chain-length poly-(3-hydroxyalkanoates) in Pseudomonas putida. The 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Aiba-Edward model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98.7%. Abdussamad et al., (2017) reported satisfactory fit on the Klebsiella sp. FIRD 2 on TBT-resistant containing lead. The Aiba-Edward model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98%. Kim et al., (2005) reported a satisfactory fit on benzene degradation. The 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. Sadhukhan et al., (2016) reported satisfactory fit of the Aiba-Edwards model on the production of succinic acid using crude and purified glycerol from a crotalaria juncea based bio refinery. The model is based on an assumption that the growth rate of an organism is proportional to the current population, and the unutilized resources in a closed habitat (Horowitz et al., 2010). The model is a substrate independent model, it describes kinetic growth based on biomass concentration only. The model accounts for inhibition of substrate (Ali et al., 2017). The Logistic model is defined by equation 15.

Where,  $ \mu $ specific growth rate, X biomass concentration,  $ X_{m} $ is the maximum biomass concentration,  $ \mu_{max} $ is the maximum specific growth rate. A number of authors have used the Logistic model to predict specific growth rate. Ardestani and Kasebkar (2018) reported a poor fit in Aspergillus niger growth. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model was produced  $ R^{2} $ of 67.7%. Abdullah et al., (2006) reported poor fit of Aspergillus oryzae in industrial natural rubber effluent serum. The Logistic model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 20.9%. Ardestani and Shafiei (2014) reported a satisfactory fit on the cell growth of Saccharomyces cerevisiae. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Logistic model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 97%. Ali et al., (2017) reported satisfactory fit of the Logistic model on ethanol production from inulin by Pichia caribbica. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model produced  $ R^{2} $ of 91%. The performance of the Logistic model was inconsistent as reported in the literature above. Although the model showed its ability to handle toxic substrate, it was never convincing. The lack of literature on the performance of this model makes it difficult to draw a conclusion on its ability to describe kinetic growth.

## Luong model

The model is a generalization of the Monod equation. The model includes a new term,  $ (1 - \frac{S}{S_m})^\alpha $. The new term is used to describe complete growth inhibition above a critical substrate concentration (Dutta et al., 2015). The model can predict substrate limitation at low and high substrate concentration accounted for by the parameter,  $ S_m $. The model is capable of predicting maximum threshold substrate concentration (Dey and Mukherjee, 2010). The Luong model is defined by equation 16.

The Luong model has been used by a number of authors as reported below and when utilized, it has performed well. Ibrahim et al., (2016) reported satisfactory fit of the Luong model in caffeine-degrading bacterium. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The OD at 620 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Luong model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98%. Ahmad et al., (2015) reported satisfactory fit of the Luong model in caffeine degradation. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Luong model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98.43%. Carrera et al. (2014) reported satisfactory fit of the Luong model in suspended and an immobilised biomass systems. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Luong model fitted suspended biomass system and immobilised biomass system with  $ R^2 $ of 80%, and 92.7% respectively. Abubakar et al. (2015) reported satisfactory fit of the Luong model in Tributyltin-resistant Klebsiella sp. Fird 2 in cadmium media. The Luong model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98.9%. The Luong model performed well in describing both toxic and non-toxic substrate as reported in the literature above. The additional new term added to the model made it to be more robust.

## Webb model

The Webb model was introduced by Edward in 1963 and is an unstructured model that describes kinetic growth based on substrate concentration only (Webb, 1963). The Webb model describes specific growth rate as a function of substrate concentration only. The model is a modified version of the Haldane model. Although the aim of the Webb model was to improve to Haldane model, Dey and Mukherjee (2010) reported that it did not improve much. It was also evident in the literature that the improvement to the Haldane model did not achieve much. Halmi et al., (2014), reported poor fit of the model on experimental data of the Catechol-degrading Candida parapsilopsis. Dutta et al., (2015) reported the Webb model is similar to the Yano Koga model. The difference between the 2 models is the term  $ (1 + \frac{S}{K_i}) $. In the Webb model the term is in the numerator and in the Yano Koga model it is in the denominator. The same observation can be said about the Haldane and the Webb model. The Haldane model does not have the term  $ (1 + \frac{S}{K_i}) $. The Webb model is defined by Eq. (17) (Dey and Mukherjee, 2010).

Where,  $ \mu $ specific growth rate,  $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate,  $ K_s $ half velocity saturation constant, S substrate concentration, and  $ K_i $ inhibition constant. A number of authors have used to Webb model with success to describe microbial kinetic growth rate. Gharibzahedi et al., (2013) reported satisfactory fit on Canthaxanthin biosynthesis by Dietzia natronolimnaea HS-1 on waste molasses hydrolysate. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Webb model produced  $ R^2 $ of 98.3%. Dutta et al., (2015) reported satisfactory fit on substrate inhibition growth kinetics for Cutinase producing Pseudomonas cepacia using Tomato peel extracted cutin. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Webb model produced  $ R^2 $ of 93.3%. Choi and Lee (2018) reported a satisfactory fit on the bioenergy production with agricultural by products. The cell dry weight method and OD at 600 nm were used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Webb model produced  $ R^2 $ of 93.6%. Mohanty et al., (2018) reported a poor fit sulphate reduction by mixed microbial culture. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Webb model produced  $ R^2 $ of 63%. Krishnan et al., (2017) reported satisfactory fit on the degradation of 3 Azo dyes RBRX-3B, DB-6 and DB-19. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The Webb model produced  $ R^2 $ of 99.9, 99.9, and 87.8% respectively. Abdussamad et al., (2017) reported satisfactory fit on lead concentration. The Webb model produced  $ R^2 $ of 83%. The Webb model performed well when fitted to both toxic and non-toxic substrate. The Webb model struggled to fit experimental data on the effects of sulphate reduction reported by Mohanty et al., (2018), while the Haldane model fitted the data with ease. Based on the

literature reported above, it could be agreed that the Webb model did not improve much on the Haldane model Dey and Mukherjee (2010).

## Conclusion

Literature shows that there are a number of unstructured models that can be used to describe kinetic growth rate. Based on the information from the literature, all the kinetic growth models were capable of describing growth rate. The only distinction is on the conducting of experiments. The collection of data, analysing of data, and environmental conditions will have an impact on the performance of each kinetic growth model. The most notable model the performed well was the Haldane model. The model was the most reported model in the literature with success on different types of substrate. The Monod, Moser, Teissier, and Contois model struggle to describe the lag and death phase during growth however they performed well as reported in the literature. The Logarithmic model was reported in the literature which concludes its incapacity to describe kinetic growth rate. The other important issue to take into consideration is the reliability of the results, sampling methods, analysing methods, and the degree of accuracy when conducting experiments. In experimental work, data is sometimes not accurate and this could be attributed primarily to the experimental cultivation systems used to collect the data, and poor selection and sensitivity of analytical methods for measuring biomass and substrate concentration.

The Powell model does not consider substrate inhibition, hence it struggles with describing the lag and death phase (Wu et al., 2018). The Powell model is defined by equation 14.
(14) \mu=\frac{(\mu_{m a x}+m)S}{K_{s}+S}-m    [code: algebraic, computes \mu]
    Where, $ \mu $ specific growth rate, $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate, $ K_s $ half saturation constant, $ S $ substrate concentration, and $ m $ constant. The Powell model has not been used widely in literature. In this paper, only 2 literatures were found of the Powell model.     The Logistic model was introduced by Pierre Verhulst in 1838 (Verhulst, 1838). The Logistic model is also known as Verhulst model (Omer, 2018). The model is based on an assumption that the growth rate of an organism is proportional to the current population, and the unutilized resources in a closed habitat (Horowitz et al., 2010). The model is a substrate independent model, it describes kinetic growth based on biomass concentration only. The model accounts for inhibition of substrate (Ali et al., 2017). The Logistic model is defined by equation 15.
(15) \mu=\mu_{max}\left[1-\frac{X}{X_{m}}\right]    [code: algebraic, computes \mu]
    Where, $ \mu $ specific growth rate, X biomass concentration, $ X_{m} $ is the maximum biomass concentration, $ \mu_{max} $ is the maximum specific growth rate. A number of authors have used the Logistic model to predict specific growth rate. Ardestani and Kasebkar (2018) reported a poor fit in Aspergillus niger growth. The cell dry weight method was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. The model was produced $ R^{2} $ of 67.7%. The model includes a new term, $ (1 - \frac{S}{S_m})^\alpha $. The new term is used to describe complete growth inhibition above a critical substrate concentration (Dutta et al., 2015). The model can predict substrate limitation at low and high substrate concentration accounted for by the parameter, $ S_m $. The model is capable of predicting maximum threshold substrate concentration (Dey and Mukherjee, 2010). The Luong model is defined by equation 16.
(16) \mu=\mu_{m a x}\frac{S}{K_{S}+S}(1-\frac{S}{S_{m}})^{n}    [code: algebraic, computes \mu]
    Where, $ \mu $ specific growth rate, $ \mu_{max} $ maximum specific growth rate, $ K_s $ half saturation constant, $ S $ substrate concentration, $ S_m $ is the critical inhibitor concentration, and $ n $ is a constant. The Luong model has been used by a number of authors as reported below and when utilized, it has performed well. Ibrahim et al., (2016) reported satisfactory fit of the Luong model in caffeine-degrading bacterium. The OD at 600 nm was used to measure the bacteria growth rates. laws.description: The Aiba–Edwards law computes bacterial specific growth rate from substrate concentration with exponential substrate inhibition.
laws.quote: The model introduces the inhibitory constant and an exponential ratio of substrate concentration and inhibitory constant (Sadhukhan et al., 2016).

laws.description: The Yano–Koga law computes specific growth rate as a substrate-dependent rate reduced by inhibition at high substrate concentration.
laws.quote: The model is capable of describing substrate inhibition effects at high substrate concentration in a continuous fermentation bioreactor (Dey and Mukherjee (2010); Dutta et al., (2015)).
laws.issue: The denominator has substrate-concentration units while \mu_{max} has time⁻¹ units, so the expression yields time⁻¹ per concentration rather than the stated specific-growth-rate units.

laws.description: The Han–Levenspiel law computes specific growth rate from substrate concentration with growth slowing or ceasing at a critical inhibitor concentration.
laws.quote: The model assumes that there is a critical inhibitor concentration where the reaction ceases or the growth rate slows down if that point is reached.

laws.description: The Powell law computes specific growth rate from substrate concentration with a cell-maintenance correction.
laws.quote: The Powell model introduces the parameter (m), which is the maintenance parameter.

laws.description: The Logistic law calculates specific growth rate from biomass concentration, declining as biomass approaches its maximum.
laws.quote: The model is a substrate independent model, it describes kinetic growth based on biomass concentration only.

assumptions.text: The model is applied to a population in a closed habitat.

laws.description: The Luong law computes specific growth rate from substrate concentration, with complete growth inhibition above a critical substrate concentration.
laws.quote: The new term is used to describe complete growth inhibition above a critical substrate concentration (Dutta et al., 2015).

laws.description: The Webb law computes specific growth rate from substrate concentration using a substrate-inhibition correction.
laws.quote: The Webb model describes specific growth rate as a function of substrate concentration only.
laws.issue: The lower-case s terms in the numerator and denominator conflict with the paper’s defined substrate symbol S; s is separately listed for the logarithmic growth law.
